slides.title: Encoding & Decoding
slides.body:
Turning Bits into Signals
Encoding: Converting 0s and 1s into actual signals such as voltage, light, or radio waves
Decoding: Converting received signals back into 0s and 1s
When the data is digital and the signal is also digital, the encoding process is called Line Coding

slides.title: 1. Unipolar
slides.body:
NRZ & Unipolar NRZ
NRZ - Non-Return to Zero:
In NRZ encoding, the signal does NOT return to zero voltage between bits. It holds its level for the entire bit period
Unipolar NRZ (Unipolar):
Uses only one polarity. 1 → +V (positive voltage); 0 → 0V (no voltage)
Simplest possible scheme. But poor DC balance - long runs of 1s produce continuous positive voltage, draining power and causing baseline drift
Rarely used today

slides.title: 2. Polar
slides.body:
NRZ-L & NRZ-I
NRZ-L (Level):
0 → low voltage (+V); 1 → high voltage (-V). Simple, but long runs of the same bit cause baseline wander and synchronization loss
NRZ-I (Invert on 1):
signal inverts on every 1; stays the same on 0. Solves sync for runs of 1s, but long runs of 0s still lose sync
The signal does not return to zero between bits - it holds its level for the full bit period

slides.title: 2. Polar

NRZ-L & NRZ-I
NRZ is bandwidth-efficient - Requires the least bandwidth of all line codes. But the synchronization problem limits its use in high-speed networks

slides.title: 2. Polar
slides.body:
RZ - Return to Zero (Polar):
The signal returns to zero voltage in the middle of every bit period
1 → starts at +V, returns to 0 at mid-bit; 0 → starts at −V, returns to 0 at mid-bit
Self-synchronizing - every bit produces a guaranteed transition.
Drawback: requires double the bandwidth of NRZ (two transitions per bit) and uses three voltage levels (+V, 0, −V) - more complex hardware

slides.title: 2. Polar (Biphase)
slides.body:
Manchester
Manchester (Polar):
Every bit period has a transition in the middle.
Rule (IEEE 802.3): 0 → high-to-low at mid-point; 1 → low-to-high at mid-point
Self-synchronizing - the mid-bit transition always occurs, regardless of the bit value
Drawback: requires double the bandwidth of NRZ
Used in: 10BASE-T Ethernet

slides.title: 2. Polar (Biphase)
slides.body:
Differential Manchester (Polar)
A transition at the start of the bit period means 0; no transition at the start means 1. A mid-bit transition always occurs (for clocking)
More noise-resistant than Manchester because the bit value is encoded by the presence or absence of a transition, not absolute voltage
Used in: Token Ring (IEEE 802.5)

slides.title: 3. Bipolar
slides.body:
AMI
AMI - Alternate Mark Inversion (Bipolar):
0 → zero voltage; 1 → alternates between +V and −V on successive 1s
Self-sync for 1s only; long runs of 0s still cause sync loss
Two consecutive same-polarity 1s indicate a transmission error (built-in error detection)
Used in: T1 telephone lines, ISDN

slides.title: 3. Bipolar
slides.body:
Pseudoternary
The exact opposite of AMI. 1 → zero voltage; 0 → alternates between +V and −V on successive 0s
Same properties as AMI (self-sync for 0s instead of 1s, same error-detection capability)
Used in: ISDN basic access lines

slides.title: Modulation & Demodulation
slides.body:
Introduction
Modulation is the process where a sender encodes data onto a high-frequency carrier wave so it can travel over wireless or bandpass communication channels. 
Demodulation is the reverse - the receiver extracts the original data from that carrier wave. 
They always work as a pair, and devices that do both are called modems (e.g., DSL modems, Wi-Fi cards, mobile radios)

slides.title: Nyquist Theorem
slides.body:
Noiseless Channel Capacity
Given a channel with a certain bandwidth, what is the maximum data rate achievable?
The answer depends on two factors: the channel bandwidth, and the number of signal levels used

slides.title: Nyquist Theorem
slides.body:
Noiseless Channel Capacity
The bandwidth of the channel in Hertz (Hz)
Number of signal levels (distinct voltage levels, phases, or symbols used)
Maximum Bit Rate  =  2  ×  Bandwidth (Hz)  ×  log₂(L)

slides.title: Nyquist Theorem
slides.body:
Noiseless Channel Capacity
Maximum data rate in bits per second (bps)
The number of bits each signal level can represent
Maximum Bit Rate  =  2  ×  Bandwidth (Hz)  ×  log₂(L)

slides.title: Nyquist Theorem
slides.body:
More signal levels mean more bits per symbol and higher data rate
But in real channels, noise makes many levels harder to distinguish
Nyquist assumes a perfect noiseless channel, which is not practical

slides.title: Solution - Maximum Capacity of a Noisy Channel
slides.body:
Shannon’s Theorem
Claude Shannon (1948) proved that every real channel - with noise - has an absolute maximum data rate beyond which reliable communication is impossible, no matter how clever the encoding or modulation. This is called the Channel Capacity

slides.title: Solution - Maximum Capacity of a Noisy Channel
slides.body:
Shannon’s Theorem
Signal-to-Noise Ratio : the ratio of signal power to noise power (unitless ratio)
Channel Capacity : the maximum achievable data rate in bits per second (bps)
Bandwidth of the channel in Hz

slides.title: Shannon’s Theorem
slides.body:
SNR and Decibels
SNR (dB)  =  10 × log₁₀(SNR)
Conversion: SNR = 30 dB
Actual SNR  =  10(30/10)  =  103  =  1000

slides.title: Shannon’s Theorem
slides.body:
Example
C  =  3000 × log₂(1 + 1000)  =  3000 × log₂(1001)  ≈  3000 × 9.97  ≈  29,900 bps
Bandwidth B = 3000 Hz. SNR = 30 dB
SNR ratio = 1000

slides.title: Nyquist & Shannon
slides.body:
Working Together
In practice, engineers use both theorems together:
Shannon gives the hard maximum data rate for a noisy channel
Nyquist shows how signal levels can help approach that limit
If Nyquist allows more than Shannon, Shannon’s limit wins

slides.title: Multiplexing - FDM, TDM, and WDM
slides.body:
Definition
Multiplexing allows multiple signals to share a single transmission medium
MUX combines signals at the sender side
DEMUX separates them at the receiver side

slides.title: Multiplexing
slides.body:
FDM
FDM
Splits bandwidth into non-overlapping frequency bands;
All senders transmit simultaneously
Guard bands prevent interference
Used in: AM/FM radio, cable TV, ADSL

slides.title: Multiplexing - FDM, TDM, and WDM
slides.body:
TDM
TDM
Each sender gets the full bandwidth for a rotating time slot
Synchronous TDM: Fixed slots per sender even if idle - simple but wasteful
Statistical TDM: Slots assigned only when there's data - efficient but needs headers to identify the source
Used in: T1/E1 lines, SONET/SDH, GSM

slides.title: Multiplexing - FDM, TDM, and WDM
slides.body:
WDM
WDM
Fibre-optic equivalent of FDM;
different wavelengths (colours) of light carry separate signals on the same fibre
DWDM packs 80–160 wavelengths, each at 10–100 Gbps → terabits/sec total
Used in: internet backbone, undersea cables

slides.title: Spread Spectrum
slides.body: FHSS and DSSS

slides.title: Spread Spectrum
slides.body:
FHSS
FHSS
Transmitter hops frequencies in a pseudo-random sequence shared with the receiver
 A jammer or eavesdropper without the key can't follow 
Used in: Bluetooth (79 channels, 1600 hops/sec), cordless phones

slides.title: Spread Spectrum
slides.body:
DSSS
Each bit is XOR'd with a high-rate chip code, spreading it across a wide band
 Receiver applies the same code to recover the bit
More chips = better noise rejection but more bandwidth
 Used in: Wi-Fi 802.11b, GPS (unique code per satellite), CDMA 2G/3G
